name: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth
summary: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth all cause rashes in children, but their other signs and the advice on getting help differ.
keyPoints: Chickenpox causes itchy spots that become blisters and then scabs, and the NHS says it usually gets better in one to two weeks.
Measles starts with cold-like signs, and a rash usually follows two to four days later.
Hand, foot and mouth disease brings mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet, and most cases clear up within about seven to ten days.
For measles, the NHS says to phone the GP or NHS 111 before going in, to avoid spreading it.
A rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis from meningitis, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: How can a parent tell these three rashes apart?
body.body:
All three illnesses can cause a rash, so the other symptoms and the pattern of the spots help to tell them apart. Chickenpox usually starts with mild flu-like symptoms such as fever, aches and loss of appetite. The rash then forms itchy spots that turn into blisters and then scabs.

Measles usually starts with cold-like signs, such as a high temperature, a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a cough, and red, sore, watery eyes. Small white spots may appear inside the mouth. The rash usually appears two to four days after the cold-like symptoms began, often on the head or neck first before spreading outwards.

Hand, foot and mouth disease often begins with a sore throat, fever and reduced appetite. A few days later come painful mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet, which can turn into blisters.

body.heading: How do the infections spread?
body.body:
The NHS says chickenpox is highly infectious and passes on through blister fluid or droplets from the nose and mouth. A person is usually contagious from about two days before the spots appear until all have formed scabs, which is usually about five days after the spots first appeared.

Measles virus is carried in tiny droplets that come out of the nose and mouth when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The NHS says it is easy to catch by breathing in these droplets. People with measles are infectious from when symptoms start until about four days after the rash first appears.

Hand, foot and mouth disease spreads through coughing, sneezing, poo and fluid from the blisters. A child can catch it more than once, because many different viruses cause it.

body.heading: What is the usual course of each illness?
body.body:
The NHS says most cases of chickenpox clear up on their own, usually within one to two weeks. Children are generally advised to stay off school or nursery until the spots have scabbed over.

With measles, a child is likely to be unwell enough to spend a few days in bed. It may take about two weeks to be well enough to return to school or nursery. Children cannot go back until four days after the rash started.

Most hand, foot and mouth cases clear up within about seven to ten days, and the mouth ulcers should pass within a week. Antibiotics do not help, because the cause is a virus.

body.heading: When should a parent phone NHS 111 or the GP?
body.body:
For chickenpox, the NHS says to get help from NHS 111 or a GP if new spots keep appearing after seven days, or if redness or pain spreads around the blisters. A GP or NHS 111 can also advise about signs of dehydration.

For measles, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if measles is suspected. It advises phoning first and not walking in, to prevent further spread. A baby with a high temperature, breathing difficulty or poor feeding should also be seen urgently.

For hand, foot and mouth disease, the NHS suggests contacting a GP if symptoms get worse or do not improve after seven to ten days. Signs of dehydration, such as sunken eyes, drowsiness or no urine for 12 hours, are also reasons to seek help.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS says a rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and to call 999 straight away. The NHS adds that the rash may not appear at all, so other signs matter too. These include a high temperature, vomiting, a headache, a stiff neck and a dislike of bright lights.

For measles, the NHS lists a seizure, severe breathing difficulty, being unable to stay awake, sudden confusion, a stiff neck or painful light sensitivity as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E. For chickenpox, the NHS lists breathing difficulty, chest pain, a seizure or a rash that does not fade under a glass as signs needing urgent help.

body.heading: What if someone is pregnant or has a weak immune system?
body.body: The NHS says pregnant women, newborn babies and people with a weakened immune system are at higher risk from chickenpox. They are advised to speak to a GP as soon as they are exposed to the virus or develop symptoms, and may need a blood test to check whether they are protected. The NHS also says to tell the receptionist that it might be chickenpox before going into a GP practice. Anyone pregnant who has been in close contact with measles is told to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111. The NHS also advises pregnant women with hand, foot and mouth disease to contact their GP.

body.heading: Can vaccination prevent these illnesses?
body.body: The NHS says the most effective way to protect a child against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine. The NHS vaccination pages now describe the MMRV vaccine, which also covers chickenpox, replacing MMR in the schedule. The NHS says older children and adults born on or before 31 December 2019 can still catch up on MMR for free. No vaccine is mentioned for hand, foot and mouth disease in the NHS pages found, so hygiene is the main prevention, including handwashing.
